title: Copper atom-pair catalyst anchored on alloy nanowires for selective and efficient electrochemical reduction of CO2
abstract: 1Department of Chemistry, Tsinghua University, Beijing, China. 2College of Materials Science and Engineering, National Base of International Sci. & Tech. Cooperation on Hybrid Materials, Qingdao University, Qingdao, China. 3College of Chemistry and Materials Science, Anhui Normal University, Wuhu, China. 4Department of Chemistry, National Taiwan University, Taipei, Taiwan. 5Beijing Synchrotron Radiation Facility, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, China. 6Department of Chemical Engineering, Tsinghua University, Beijing, China. 7Center for Catalytic Science and Technology, Department of Chemical and Biomolecular Engineering, University of Delaware, Newark, Delaware, USA. 8These authors contributed equally: Jiqing Jiao, Rui Lin, Shoujie Liu and Weng-Chon Cheong. *e-mail: haixiao@tsinghua.edu.cn; cchen@mail.tsinghua.edu.cn The overdependence on fossil fuels has led to an excessive emission of the greenhouse gas CO2, and thus there is a pressing demand to develop a highly efficient and selective technology for the reduction of CO2 to realize a sustainable carbon-cycle utilization1. Among all the efforts, the electrochemical reduction of CO2 (CO2RR) presents a promising route that delivers useful single-carbon chemicals (C1) and multicarbon (C2 and C3) fuels, and potentially serves as a supplement to the petrochemical feedstock2. To date, a wealth of catalytically active materials has been scrutinized for their performances for CO2RR, such as metals3–18, alloys19–24, metal oxides25 and metal/metal oxide composites26–29. However, these catalysts generally face issues regarding overpotentials, selectivity and an undesired competing hydrogen evolution reaction (HER); therefore, it is still an urgent task to develop advanced electrocatalysts with high performances for CO2RR. Single-atom and/or single-site catalysts have found extensive applications in electrochemical catalysis by virtue of their extremely high atom utilization and exceptional catalytic performances36. Yet still, the catalytically active centre therein, owing to its simplicity in structure, is usually only capable of catalysing single-molecule elementary reactions, whereas the activation step in most catalytic reactions usually involves multiple molecules. For example, in CO2RR, although CO2 is the only species to be activated, the synergistic adsorption of H2O and CO2 molecules plays a vital role33. Therefore, it is desirable to construct ‘atomic interfaces’ (typically between two atoms with different charges or even different chemical identities) with higher complexities and more sophisticated functionalities, so as to extend the relevant applications to catalytic reactions that simultaneously require different kinds of functional active sites. Here we report an atom-pair catalyst (APC) that features a highly active atomic interface. The active site of APC comprises Cu1–Cu1 pairs stabilized by the Te surface defects on Pd10Te3 alloy nanowires. We demonstrate its high activity and Faradaic efficiency to selectively produce CO (FECO) in CO2RR at low applied overpotentials. The competing HER is almost completely suppressed when an APC is used; in sharp contrast, HER dominates when the pure Pd10Te3 nanowire is used as catalyst. The experimental results and density functional theory (DFT) calculations indicate that the Cu1–Cu1 site in an APC promotes the CO2 activation via a ‘biatomic activating bimolecular’ mechanism. Our work here offers an ideal model of interface design at the atomic level, because the afforded APC features two different atomic centres to adsorb two different molecules. We believe the concept of APC is an effective and competent supplement to single-atom catalysis, and will provide numerous new opportunities for atomic-level dispersed catalysts to be applied in more complex catalytic reactions.

The overdependence on fossil fuels has led to an excessive emis-sion of the greenhouse gas CO2, and thus there is a pressing demand to develop a highly efficient and selective technology for the reduction of CO2 to realize a sustainable carbon-cycle utilization1. Among all the efforts, the electrochemical reduction of CO2 (CO2RR) presents a promising route that delivers useful single-carbon chemicals (C1) and multicarbon (C2 and C3) fuels, and potentially serves as a supplement to the petrochemical feedstock2. However, these catalysts generally face issues regarding overpotentials, selectivity and an undesired competing hydrogen evolution reaction (HER); therefore, it is still an urgent task to develop advanced electrocatalysts with high performances for CO2RR5,8,12,30–35.
Single-atom and/or single-site catalysts have found extensive applications in electrochemical catalysis by virtue of their extremely high atom utilization and exceptional catalytic performances36. Yet still, the catalytically active centre therein, owing to its simplicity in structure, is usually only capable of catalysing single-molecule elementary reactions, whereas the activation step in most catalytic reactions usually involves multiple molecules. For example, in CO2RR, although CO2 is the only species to be activated, the synergistic adsorption of H2O and CO2 molecules plays a vital role33. Therefore, it is desirable to construct ‘atomic interfaces’ (typically between two atoms with different charges or even different
chemical identities) with higher complexities and more sophisticated functionalities, so as to extend the relevant applications to catalytic reactions that simultaneously require different kinds of functional active sites.
Here we report an atom-pair catalyst (APC) that features a highly active atomic interface. The active site of APC comprises Cu10–Cu1x+ pairs stabilized by the Te surface defects on Pd10Te3 alloy nanowires. sections.text:
The electrochemical reduction of CO2 could play an important role in addressing climate-change issues and global energy demands as part of a carbon-neutral energy cycle. Single-atom catalysts can display outstanding electrocatalytic performance; however, given their single-site nature they are usually only amenable to reactions that involve single molecules. For processes that involve multiple molecules, improved catalytic properties could be achieved through the development of atomically dispersed catalysts with higher complexities. Here we report a catalyst that features two adjacent copper atoms, which we call an ‘atom-pair catalyst’, that work together to carry out the critical bimolecular step in CO2 reduction. The atom-pair catalyst features stable Cu10–Cu1x+ pair structures, with Cu1x+ adsorbing H2O and the neighbouring Cu10 adsorbing CO2, which thereby promotes CO2 activation. This results in a Faradaic efficiency for CO generation above 92%, with the competing hydrogen evolution reaction almost completely suppressed. Experimental characterization and density functional theory revealed that the adsorption configuration reduces the activation energy, which generates high selectivity, activity and stability under relatively low potentials.

Supplementary Information. One-dimensional Pd10Te3 alloy nanowires were synthesized based on a reported method37,38. Samples with varying Cu loadings were prepared by controlling the introduced amount of Cu precursors, and the actual loading ratios were determined by inductively coupled plasma mass spectroscopy, as listed in Supplementary Table 1. The morphology, crystal structure and elemental distribution of the as-synthesized catalyst are summarized in Fig. 1b–g. The scanning electron microscopy image (Fig. 1b) shows the ultrathin Cu-doped Pd10Te3 nanowires spread over a micrometre-scale area. The transmission electron microscopy image (Fig. 1c) reveals that the one-dimensional nanowires are well dispersed and uniform in diameter (~5 nm). The X-ray diffraction patterns of pure and Cu-doped (0.10%) nanowires are quite similar (Supplementary Fig. 1), both indexed as cubic Pd10Te3 (JCPDS No. 65-4540). The X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy for nanowire samples with different Cu loadings also reveals similar profiles for Pd as well as for Te, with no noticeable signals of Cu (owing to the low loading ratios) (Supplementary Fig. 2). The high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) image (Fig. 1d) of a selected area shows clear lattice fringes with distances of 0.22, 0.26 and 0.31 nm, which correspond to the (440), (422) and (400) facets, respectively, of cubic Pd10Te3. We can therefore conclude that the nanowires grow along the < 110> direction. In addition, the nanowire surface is rough, with obvious crystal defects. Likewise, the aberration-corrected high-angle annular dark-field scanning transmission electron microscopy (HAADF-STEM) image (Fig. 1e) also reveals the abundant crystal defects on the edge of the nanowires. Supplementary Fig. 3 summarizes the aberration-corrected HRTEM images of pure Pd10Te3 and different Cu-doped nanowires, which confirm the same crystal structures. The elemental distribution of the trace amount of Cu on the Pd10Te3 nanowires was confirmed by energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) line scanning (Fig. 1f). Along the transverse direction of five parallel nanowires, the X-ray counts of Pd, Te and Cu fluctuate in a similar manner, indicating the uniform distribution of Cu on Pd10Te3 nanowires (Supplementary Fig. 4). In contrast, for undoped Pd10Te3 nanowires, no signal of Cu was detected (Supplementary Fig. 5). Furthermore, atomic-resolution EDS mapping also confirmed the existence of Cu on the doped nanowires (Fig. 1g). Notice that a number of O atoms were found to be accompanying the Cu atoms, which gives us an important hint for the subsequent clarification of the precise atomic configuration of the active sites. Assessment on CO2RR performances of the catalysts. To investigate the effect of the trace amount of Cu on the electrochemical performance, we carried out CO2RR assessments on pure and doped nanowires using a hydrogen cell (separated by Nafion 117) filled with 0.2 M NaHCO3 solution (pH = 7), and we used the

current density and Faradaic efficiency of the reduction products as the indices to evaluate the performance. As revealed by the linear sweep voltammetry curves (Fig. 2a), undoped Pd10Te3 nanowires delivered a total current density of 2.70 mA cm−2 at − 0.98 V (versus RHE), which indicates a rather low activity. With the introduction of a trace amount of Cu (loadings of 0.02, 0.06, 0.10 and 0.16%), the total current density was significantly elevated. Notably, the sample with a 0.10% Cu loading delivered 18.74 mA cm−2 at − 0.98 V (versus RHE), 6.94 times as high as that for undoped nanowires. When the Cu loading went higher to 0.20%, the current density dropped to 2.66 mA cm−2, even lower than that for undoped nanowires.
Apart from current density, the selectivity in CO2RR was also investigated. We tested all the samples under potentials of − 0.66 V, − 0.78 V, − 0.87 V and − 0.98 V (Fig. 2b), and obtained the corresponding Faradaic efficiency values. In aqueous electrolytes, CO2RR generally suffers from a competing HER, particularly when a Pd-based catalyst is used. For our catalysts here, we found no products other than CO and H2 within the tested potential range
(Supplementary Table 2). As Fig. 2b,c clearly shows, the FECO values for undoped nanowires under applied potentials are all below 17%, and the corresponding Faradaic efficiency for H2 (FEH2) values are relatively high. For the five doped samples, the FECO values are all superior to those for undoped nanowires. Again, 0.10% proved to be the optimal loading ratio. At − 0.78 V, the sample with a 0.10% Cu loading displayed a FECO of 92%, 6.57 times as high as that for undoped nanowires (14%); the corresponding FEH2 was merely 3%, which implies that the HER activity was substantially suppressed with a relatively low Cu loading.
Combining the data of total current density and FECO, we obtained the CO current densities under different potentials. As shown in Fig. 2d, the sample with a 0.10% Cu loading delivers a CO current density far higher than those of the other samples under every potential. At − 0.78 V, the CO current density is 8.6 mA cm−2, 57 times as high as that for undoped sample (0.15 mA cm−2), which indicates a drastically elevated CO2RR activity. The current density remained virtually unchanged, and the FECO showed only a small decline from the initial 92% to the final 80%, indicative of a still relatively high CO selectivity. As revealed in Supplementary Fig. 6, the morphology of the Cu-doped Pd10Te3 nanowires was well retained after deposition onto carbon paper. Therefore, the introduction of 0.10% Cu not only altered the electrochemical catalytic pathways for Pd-based catalysts, but also improved the stability in CO2RR. (As is discussed later, the sample with 0.10% Cu loading is the Cu–APC mentioned above.)
Fitting of XAFS spectroscopy and theoretical calculation on Cu–APC structure. As shown in the above data, the CO2RR catalytic performance is extremely sensitive to the Cu loading ratio. To unearth the underpinning mechanism, we need to clarify the status of Cu on the surface of the Pd10Te3 nanowires, for which we conducted synchrotron radiation-based X-ray absorption fine structure (XAFS) spectroscopy39. Figure 3a shows the K-edge X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES) spectra of nanowire samples with different Cu loadings (0.10, 0.16 and 0.20%), as well as the spectra of CuO, Cu2O and Cu foil as references. The absorption edge positions of all three doped nanowire samples are located between that of Cu and CuO, which suggests that on average the Cu atoms are positively charged and the valence state of Cu is between 0 and + 2 (Fig. 3a). The Fourier-transformed k3-weighted spectra (Fig. 3b) of the nanowire samples showed three main peaks at 1.62, 1.90 and 2.10 Å, which correspond to the Cu–O, Cu–Cu and Cu–Pd coordination shells, respectively. It can be seen that, as the Cu loading increases, the intensity of the Cu–O peak (at 1.62 Å) is elevated, whereas the Cu–Cu peak (at 1.90 Å) gradually decreases and the Cu–Pd peak (at 2.10 Å) also emerges and is enhanced with an increased Cu loading. The wavelet transform plot (Fig. 3c) shows that the maximum of the wavelet transform of Cu–APC is at 5~6 Å−1, which corresponds to Cu–O and Cu–Cu bonding; the maximum of the wavelet transform plot of Cu foil is 6~8 Å−1, which corresponds to Cu–Cu bonding. Compared with that of Cu foil, the slight shift of the wavelet transform maximum of Cu–APC may be due to the low coordination number of Cu–O and the contraction of Cu–Cu bond in the Cu–APC. All the above data suggest that, as the Cu loading increases from 0.10% to 0.20%, CuOx (Cu–O) and CuPdx (Cu–Pd) species were formed, whereas Cux (Cu–Cu) species gradually disappeared. To verify this inference, we conducted EXAFS fitting to unveil the quantitative coordination configuration of Cu atoms (Supplementary Fig. 7). From Supplementary Table 3, the fitting results show that the Cu–Cu bond length in the 0.10% doped sample is 2.49 Å, shorter than that for Cu foil (2.56 Å), and the Cu–Cu coordination number is 2.1, much smaller than that of Cu foil (12), which suggests that Cu exists as Cux and displays atomic-level dispersion in the defects of Pd10Te3. The average Cu–O bond length is 1.89 Å, shorter than r(Cu–O) in CuO (1.98 Å)33, which indicates that the Cux was protected by O atom, yet not in the form of CuO or Cu2O. When the loading ratio goes to 0.20%, the Cu-Cu coordination number drops to 0, and the Cu–O bond length increases to 1.97 Å, very close to that in CuO (1.98 Å); the Cu–O coordination number increases to 2.7, which indicates that for the sample with a 0.20% Cu loading, Cu exists in the form of CuO. In addition, the Pd peaks in R-space spectra (Supplementary Fig. 8) shift as the Cu loading increases, which also verifies the formation of the Pd–Cu bond after Cu doping.
To clarify further the value of x in Cux, we conducted theoretical calculation of XANES spectra (Fig. 3d). By comparing the XANES experimentally recorded for Cu–APC and theoretically calculated for Cu4, C13, Cu19 and Cu43 (ref. 40) we found that Cu–APC and Cu4 displayed very similar spectral profiles, from which we inferred that x ≈ 4 (3, 4, 5). In addition, for the model obtained by DFT calculation (vide infra), the Cu–Cu bond length is 2.52 Å, also in good consistency with the data obtained by the EXAFS fitting (2.49 Å) (Supplementary Table 4).
In addition, we employed in situ characterization techniques to investigate the behaviour of Cu species in CO2RR. In situ XANES spectra (Supplementary Figs. 9–11) showed that CuOx (Cu–O) species could retain their stability during the electrochemical tests (even under a potential of − 0.98 V). In situ attenuated total reflection surface-enhanced infrared absorption spectroscopy (Supplementary Figs. 12 and 13) revealed that, compared to pure Pd10Te3 and 0.20 wt% Cu-loaded Pd10Te3 nanowires, the Cu–APC sample showed a distinct peak at 2,100–2,080 cm−1 at 0 to − 0.5 V versus RHE, which suggests that the Cu–APC sample features unique sites that are absent in the other two samples.
From the above data, it can be concluded that, in the Cu–APC sample (0.10% Cu), Cu is atomically dispersed and partially oxidized to Cux+, probably in the form Cu4–Ox, whereas for the sample with 0.20% loading, Cu exists in a form analogous to CuO. Notably, the EXAFS fitting (Fig. 3c and Supplementary Fig. 7) gives bond lengths (for Cu–O, Cu–Cu and Cu–Pd) very close to those obtained by DFT calculation (vide infra), and thereby adds more validity to our conclusion above. Combining the afore-discussed data in CO2RR catalysis, it can be inferred that the Cu4–Ox structure is the essential active site for converting CO2 into CO in CO2RR.
For the postulated Cu4–Ox structure in the Cu–APC sample, to gain further insight on its precise atomic configuration, we carried out theoretical calculations and obtained a structural model of Cu atoms on Pd10Te3 nanowires (Fig. 3d). The (110) surface slab is adopted as it is the most stable surface for cubic Pd10Te3. During the preparation process, some Te atoms are etched by NaOH, and the vacancy on the surface presents a natural and ideal host for O atoms. Thus, we looked into a Pd10Te3 surface with a Te atom replaced by O (Fig. 3e). The doped Cu atoms then bind with the O atoms to form a thermodynamically stable configuration. The calculations reveal that Cu4 is the smallest stable configuration (Fig. 3f,g), with one Cu atom binding with O to form Cu1x+, which further binds with a neighbouring Cu atom to form a Cu10–Cu1x+ atom pair (Cu–APC). In CO2RR, it is these two Cu atoms in the Cu–APC that directly participate in the electrocatalysis, whereas the other two underlying Cu atoms accommodate the defects around the vacancyoccupying O atom, which stabilizes the Cu–APC. Subsequently, we increased the number of Cu atoms from four to eight, and the Cu10–Cu1x+ atom pair still turned out to be the essential active site, with only a small change in the reaction free energy for CO2 activation (Supplementary Table 5). These results are in good accordance with the XAFS fitting discussed above; also, these results explain well the fact that Cu atoms were found to be accompanying the O atoms in atomic-resolution EDS mapping (Fig. 1g). Therefore, it is reasonable to claim that Cu10–Cu1x+ atom pair is the essential catalytically active site in CO2RR.
CO2 activation on the Cu–APC catalyst. Figure 4a shows the calculated free energy profiles at U = − 0.78 V for CO2 activation on the classic Cu metal catalyst, the Cu metal embedded in the Cu2O (Cu@Cu2O) catalyst and the Cu–APC reported here. Compared to the Cu metal catalyst, both Cu@Cu2O and Cu–APC improve the kinetics and thermochemistry of CO2 activation, because these two catalysts provide two intrinsically different sites to bind the CO2 and the H2O, respectively, which stabilizes the negative charge on chemisorbed CO2 (also known as the interface approach). And, notably, the Cu–APC shows an even better improvement than the Cu@ Cu2O catalyst, because it reduces the size of the catalytic interface down to between two single atoms (hence, atomic interface), which offers stronger bonding due to unsaturation. We further found a correlation between the Lewis acidity of surface H2O and the catalytic activity (Supplementary Table 6), which is consistent with the underlying mechanism.
Note that instead of the proton-coupled electron transfer process41, a Volmer-like electron step as the rate-determining

Compared with pure Pd10Te3 nanowires, Cu–APC displayed a lower free energy barrier (∆ G), which suggests better kinetics (Supplementary Fig. 15). We also found that the Cu–APC catalyst effectively suppresses HER and further reduction of CO in terms of the hydrogen adsorption energy42 (Supplementary Table 7) and CO hydrogenation energy43 (Supplementary Table 8). Therefore, we believe that the Cu–APC could serve as an example model for designing a highly selective and efficient CO2RR catalyst.
In the experiments, a further increase in the Cu loading leads to a significant decline in performance. This is probably because the excess Cu atoms then cover the APC surface. These extra Cu atoms are prone to further oxidation to CuO (Fig. 3), which is subsequently
reduced back to Cu during CO2RR. Its catalytic performance is expected to be similar to that of the Cu metal catalyst, which has been extensively studied by experiments44 and calculations45.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text:
In this work, we demonstrate a strategy to construct a Cu atom-pair site that is anchored on Pd10Te3 alloy nanowires. At the optimal Cu loading ratio (0.10%), one in every four Cu atoms binds with O to form Cu1x+, which, in association with a neighbouring Cu10 atom, forms a stable Cu10–Cu1x+ atom-pair structure. In the critical step of CO2 reduction, the H2O molecule adsorbed on Cu1x+ stabilizes the CO2 molecule chemisorbed on the neighbouring Cu10, and thereby promotes CO2 activation. This leads to a FECO of over 92%, and the competing HER is almost completely suppressed. sections.heading: Methods
sections.text:
Preparation of Cu–APC (Cu 0.10 wt%) on Pd10Te3 nanowires. An H2PdCl4 aqueous solution (40 ml, 25 mM) and a Cu(NO3)2 aqueous solution (5 ml, 5 mM) was added into 50 ml of a Te nanowire aqueous solution under magnetic stirring at room temperature for 12 h. Acetone (as the flocculant) was added into the above solution, and the product was collected by centrifugation. Then the product was dispersed into a 0.01 M NaOH solution with vigorous magnetic stirring, and further stirred for 12 h. The solid product was separated by centrifugation and washed three times with 0.01 M HCl solution and deionized water. The detailed preparation procedures for pure the Pd10Te3 nanowires and Cu-loaded Pd10Te3 nanowires with different loadings (0.02 wt%, 0.16 wt% and 0.20 wt%) is given in the Supplementary Information.
CO2 electrochemical reduction. A 0.2 M sodium bicarbonate aqueous solution was used as the electrolyte for the CO2 electroreduction. The electrolyte was prepared by bubbling CO2 into the sodium carbonate aqueous solution overnight. All the water used in the CO2RR was ultrapure water (18.2 MΩ cm). A hydrogentype cell was used as the electrolyser. A Nafion 117 membrane was inserted between the cathodic and anodic chambers. A mass flow controller was used to set the CO2 flow rate at 20 sccm. The working electrode, counter electrode and reference electrode were Sigracet 39 BC carbon paper, Pt wire and Ag/AgCl, respectively. The CO2 was bubbled into the sodium bicarbonate electrolyte for 2 h before electrolysis. The linear sweep voltammetry curves were recorded with a Princeton PMC-500 electrochemical workstation with a scan rate of 10 mV s–1. All the potentials were reported with respect to the RHE and corrected by IR drop compensation. The chronoamperometry tests were conducted at each potential
for 40 min. The long-term stability measurement was operated at the potential of − 0.78 V versus RHE for 3 h. The gas products of CO2RR were detected dynamically on the Shimazu 2010 plus gas chromatography equipped with a BID detector and ShinCarbon ST 100/120 packed column. High-purity helium (99.9999%) was used as the carrier gas for the chromatography. The Faradaic efficiency of each gas product was calculated by the equation:

The liquid products of electrolysis were analysed by a Bruker Avance III HD 400 NMR spectroscope.
Both CO2 reduction and HER make contributions to the current in an aqueous electrolyte. The reduction products were detected by gas chromatography and NMR spectroscopy for the calculation of Faradaic efficiency to accurately evaluate the CO2RR activity. No liquid products were detected after electrolysis.
XAFS measurements. The XAFS spectra were obtained at 1W1B station in BSRF (Beijing Synchrotron Radiation Facility, China) operated at 2.5 GeV with a maximum current of 250 mA. XAFS measurements at the Cu K edge were performed in fluorescence mode using a Lytle detector. All the samples were pelletized as disks of 8 mm diameter and 1 mm thickness. The XAFS spectra of the Cu K edge for the sample were collected several times to obtain high-quality data. XAFS spectra of Pd were recorded at the SP8 (Japan) 12B2 Taiwan beamline of the National Synchrotron Radiation Research Center (NSRRC); the electron storage ring was operated at 8.0 GeV with a constant current of ~100 mA.
